summary.summary: Blackpool's year-end treasury report is routine and shows the council actively cutting borrowing costs, not adding risk. During 2025/26 it refinanced £110m of short-term borrowing into long-term debt to rebalance the book to a 50:50 long/short split, repaid £5.93m of long-term loans, and deferred the rest of the year's capital borrowing requirement until rates look favourable. That mix cut the overall pooled borrowing rate to 4.26% from 4.58% the year before (General Fund pool 3.82%, HRA pool 4.47%). The treasury revenue account came in £830k over its £26.666m budget (3.1%), driven mainly by an HRA interest shortfall (£392k) and lower loans interest receivable (£588k) after some loans were renegotiated at year-end; investment earnings were £242k. No CFR, year-end debt total, investment balances or prudential-indicator compliance detail are in this excerpt — those sit in Appendices 4a-4d, which are referenced but not included in the packet.
summary.as_of_doc: Treasury Management Outturn for the Year Ended 31 March 2026

signals.headline: Modest 3.1% treasury revenue overspend (£830k on £26.666m budget); no new net borrowing, pooled rate falling (4.58% to 4.26%)
signals.why: Nothing in this outturn report points to distress — borrowing was restructured to reduce future cost, not increased.

news_drafts.headline: Blackpool's £7.3m schools-grant deficit to be 90% written off by new High Needs Stability Grant
news_drafts.lead:
Blackpool Council's dedicated schools grant reserve stood at a deficit of £7.331m at 31 March 2026, and a one-off High Needs Stability Grant will write off 90% of it, according to the month 5 financial monitoring report to the Executive for 2026/27. The dedicated schools grant is the government grant that funds schools. The council is responsible for the remaining 10%.

The paper says the new grant replaces the Safety Valve Programme. It says the Department for Education has not yet confirmed whether deficits accrued in 2026/27 and beyond will be covered by future grant payments.

The children's services appendix to the report sets out how the grant is treated from here. It says "Any under or overspends against services funded by the DSG will be carried forward to 2027/28", and that overspends are the first call on that year's grant. The education line funded by the grant is forecast to overspend by £1.585m for 2026/27. The forecast carry-forward balance on the grant is £8.969m.

news_drafts.headline: Blackpool plans SEND specialist base at St Mary's Catholic Academy, paid for from £1.9m allowance
news_drafts.lead:
Blackpool Council's Executive had before it, at its meeting on 12 October 2026, a paper proposing a specialist base at St Mary's Catholic Academy for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), meaning children who need extra help at school because of a learning difficulty or disability. The paper says the project will be fully funded by the council, using the 2026-27 High Needs Provision Capital Allowance of £1.9m.

That allowance is capital funding, money for things that last, and the paper describes it as the Department for Education's allocation to Blackpool for high needs, the part of school funding for children with SEND. Recommendation 2.3 in the paper refers to the same money as the department's SEND Capital Grant. The paper does not say how much of the £1.9m would remain after this scheme.

The paper also expects a benefit in transport. It says shorter distances should reduce the cost of SEND home-to-school transport and the impact on the core funded transport budget, and it refers to "additional benefits of shorter and less expensive SEND home-to-school transport plans". It gives no figure for the expected saving.
news_drafts.paper_title: ESTABLISHMENT OF A SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS AND DISABILITIES (SEND) SPECIALIST BASE AT ST MARY'S CATHOLIC ACADEMY

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9(a) Blackpool Council Annual Auditors Report 1011
findings.headline: The Government's IDACI-based funding methodology change reduced the anticipated funding outcome for Blackpool relative to earlier modelling.
findings.detail: The paper says the methodology was amended at a late stage to include the Income Deprivation Affecting Children Index, which materially altered the distribution of resources. The Council says it faces a significant gap between assessed need and available resources.
findings.matters: Late methodology changes that cut funding are a risk for every council modelling its medium-term plan on pre-reform assumptions.
findings.quote: This change materially altered the distribution of resources and reduced the anticipated funding outcome for Blackpool relative to earlier modelling and expectations.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9(a) Blackpool Council Annual Auditors Report 1011
findings.headline: The Council's new Section 151 Officer appointment is listed as an early action following the May 2026 corporate peer review.
findings.detail: The paper lists the appointment of a new Section 151 Officer, a Transformation Board and strengthened governance among early actions. The Council's recommendation response gives the Section 151 Officer as the responsible officer for the financial sustainability recovery plan, with a due date of March 2027.
findings.matters: A change of S151 officer during a financial recovery is a change a lender or peer council will track against the March 2027 deadline.
findings.quote: Early actions include the appointment of a new Section 151 Officer

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9(a) Blackpool Council Annual Auditors Report 1011
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer concluded in February 2026 Section 25 Statement on 2026/27 budget; savings delivery was 71% in each of last two years
findings.detail: The auditor records that the budget depends on savings delivery, the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy, spending within cash limits and rebuilding working balances. The auditor says there remains significant uncertainty over the Council's ability to deliver balanced budgets without continued reliance on reserves.
findings.matters: A Section 25 statement's own wording on robustness and adequacy is the formal test a finance director at another council would read against their own.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget approved February 2026; 71% savings delivery in each of the last two years
findings.quote: The Section 151 Officer concluded, in the Section 25 Statement that went to the Budget Council in February 2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9(a) Blackpool Council Annual Auditors Report 1011
findings.headline: Several of the council's seven wholly owned subsidiaries continue to report recurring losses, deficit reserve positions and reliance on council support.
findings.detail: The auditor says several subsidiaries have loans with the Council and expects the Council to closely monitor the financial sustainability of these entities and their implications for the wider Group.
findings.matters: Loans to companies with deficit reserves are a direct credit exposure, and peers with similar group structures will want to see how oversight is run.
findings.figures: Seven wholly owned companies; at least twice-yearly Shareholder Committee updates
findings.quote: Several subsidiary companies continue to operate in challenging financial circumstances, with recurring losses, deficit reserve positions and reliance on Council support evident across parts of the Group.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9(a) Blackpool Council Annual Auditors Report 1011
findings.headline: KPMG has not yet reached its conclusions on the 2025/26 financial statements and other information.
findings.detail: The auditor issued this report before completing work on the financial statements and other information, to meet the 30 November deadline. The Whole of Government Accounts procedures also remain unconfirmed.
findings.matters: Any opinion on the 2025/26 accounts remains open, which affects lenders and peers relying on the published figures.
findings.figures: Auditor's Annual Report due no later than 30 November each year
findings.quote: Consequently, we have not reached our conclusions in respect of these areas.

daily_post.headline: Council Tax collection stood at 42.7% at month 5, with £35.8m collected, against 42.6% a year earlier.
daily_post.lead: A council ranked among the lowest in England for Council Tax collection shows a weak income base, which a lender would weigh against the reserves that cover it.
